name: Kublai Khan
info: Kublai Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, became Great Khan of the Mongols in 1260, founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and by 1279 completed the conquest of the Song, becoming the first non-Han emperor of all China.

facts.born: 23 September 1215; the fourth son of Tolui, and his second by his chief wife Sorghaghtani Beki; a grandson of Genghis Khan, of the House of Borjigin
facts.died: 18 February 1294, aged 78, after a long decline in health with gout and diabetes; taken for burial to the burial place of the Khans in Mongolia
facts.role: Viceroy over northern China (from 1251); Great Khan (Khagan) of the Mongol Empire (1260–1294); founder and first emperor of the Yuan dynasty (1271–1294), temple name Shizu, regnal name Setsen Khan
facts.known: founding the Yuan dynasty; completing the conquest of the Song dynasty; the capitals Dadu (Khanbaliq, modern Beijing) and Shangdu (Xanadu); a unified paper currency; the failed invasions of Japan, Vietnam and Java; patronage of the Phags pa Lama and of Muslim scientists; receiving Marco Polo

t: Kublai's proclamation as Great Khan in 1260, against the election of his brother Ariq Böke, led to a civil war lasting until 1264 and marked the beginning of the division of the Mongol Empire.
He made China his base, proclaimed the dynastic name Great Yuan in 1271 and destroyed the Song by 1279, becoming the first non-Han emperor to rule all of China proper.
His invasions of Japan, Vietnam and Java failed or won only nominal submission, and their cost, with the expansion of paper currency, caused inflation.
dyk: In August 1260 Kublai created the first unified paper currency, the Jiaochao, circulated throughout his domain with no expiration date; he is considered to be the first maker of fiat money.
ev: Kublai is born, a son of Tolui and Sorghaghtani Beki and a grandson of Genghis Khan
Ordered by his brother Möngke to attack Yunnan, he takes the capital of the Dali Kingdom and spares its residents
A kurultai in his own territories proclaims him Great Khan, although another at Karakorum has already named his brother Ariq Böke
Ariq Böke surrenders to Kublai at Xanadu, ending the civil war
Kublai officially creates the Yuan dynasty, proclaiming Dadu, modern Beijing, the capital the following year
The Song are destroyed at the Battle of Yamen, where the last Song emperor Zhao Bing dies by jumping into the sea
The second invasion of Japan fails and its fleet is destroyed; his wife Chabi dies the same year
Kublai dies at the age of 78, having passed the seal of Crown Prince to his grandson Temür

sections.early:
Kublai was born on 23 September 1215, the fourth son of Tolui and his second by his chief wife Sorghaghtani Beki, and a grandson of Genghis Khan. On his grandfather's advice his mother chose a Buddhist Tangut woman as his nurse, whom he later honoured highly. In 1224, near the Ili River, Genghis Khan performed a ceremony over his grandsons Möngke and Kublai after their first hunt, in which the nine-year-old Kublai had helped to kill a rabbit and an antelope. Genghis Khan died in 1227, and Tolui served as regent for two years until Kublai's uncle Ogedei was enthroned as Khagan in 1229. Tolui died in 1232.

After the Mongol conquest of the Jin dynasty Ogedei in 1236 gave Hebei to the family of Tolui, and Kublai received an estate of his own with 10,000 households. Inexperienced, he gave local officials free rein; corruption and aggressive taxation drove large numbers of Han peasants to flee and tax revenues fell. Kublai came to his appanage and ordered reforms, his mother sent new officials, the tax laws were revised and many of those who had fled returned.

The most prominent element of his early life was his study of, and strong attraction to, contemporary Han culture. He invited Haiyun, the leading Buddhist monk of northern China, to his ordo in Mongolia and questioned him on Buddhism at Karakorum in 1242; Haiyun named Kublai's son Zhenjin and introduced him to the monk Liu Bingzhong, a painter, calligrapher, poet and mathematician who became his adviser. The Shanxi scholar Zhao Bi joined his entourage, as did men of other nationalities.
sections.rise:
When his eldest brother Möngke became Khan of the Mongol Empire in 1251, Kublai received the viceroyalty over northern China and moved his ordo to central Inner Mongolia. He raised the agricultural output of Henan and increased welfare spending, acts acclaimed by Han warlords. In 1253, ordered to attack Yunnan, he took the Dali capital and spared its residents although the ruling Gao family had killed his envoys. Officials jealous of his success said he dreamed of an empire of his own, and in 1257 Möngke sent two inspectors who listed 142 breaches of regulations, executed some Han officials and abolished his pacification commission; Kublai appealed in person and Möngke publicly forgave him. In 1258 Kublai presided over a conference of Taoists and Buddhists, after which he forcibly converted 237 Taoist temples to Buddhism.

Möngke died in 1259 while Kublai was marching to join him against the Song. Kublai kept the death secret, besieged Wuchang and reached a peace agreement with the Song minister Jia Sidao. Warned by his wife that his younger brother Ariq Böke was raising troops, he went north and learned that a kurultai at Karakorum had named Ariq Böke Great Khan with the support of most of Genghis Khan's descendants. Kublai summoned his own kurultai, less well attended, which proclaimed him Great Khan on 15 April 1260. In the war that followed Karakorum was destroyed, Kublai cut off its food supplies, and Ariq Böke surrendered at Xanadu on 21 August 1264. Kublai pardoned him but executed his chief supporters.
sections.deeds:
Kublai treated China as his main base and adopted Chinese political and cultural models. In August 1260 he created a unified paper currency, convertible with silver and gold. In 1271 he gave the Mongol regime in China the name Dai Yuan, and the following year proclaimed Dadu, known to the Mongols as Khanbaliq, in modern Beijing, the capital; Shangdu, also called Xanadu, was his summer capital. Most of the domains were administered as provinces, each with a governor and vice-governor. He rebuilt the Grand Canal, repaired public buildings and extended highways, and the record of the Mongols lists 20,166 public schools created in his reign.

After the fall of Xiangyang in 1273, where the trebuchets of the siege engineers Ismail and Al al-Din were used, he made Bayan of the Baarin supreme commander against the Song. The Song imperial family surrendered in 1276, and in 1279 the last Song loyalists were crushed at the Battle of Yamen. Goryeo, invaded and made a tributary state in 1260, came under tighter control after 1273.

He appointed the Sakya lama Phagpa his Imperial Preceptor, with power over all the empire's Buddhist monks. Thirty Muslims served as high officials at his court and eight of the twelve administrative districts had Muslim governors; Muslim astronomers such as Jamal ad-Din introduced instruments that allowed the Chinese calendar to be corrected, while the astronomer and engineer Guo Shoujing built a 30 km channel to supply Dadu with water. Several Europeans visited the empire, notably Marco Polo in the 1270s, who lived in the emperor's lands for 17 years.
sections.opponents:
Kublai's accession was contested from the start: Ariq Böke had been elected by the representatives of Genghis Khan's four elder sons. Mongol traditionalists condemned his move to Khanbaliq and his ties to Han culture, asking “What will happen to the old customs?”, and an uprising in Karakorum was barely contained. Kaidu of the House of Ögedei, who refused to attend his court, declared himself the legitimate heir in place of a khan who had turned from the ways of Genghis Khan; he defeated Yuan armies, took Almaliq and briefly occupied Karakorum in 1289. In 1287 the prince Nayan, threatened by Kublai's bureaucratisation, revolted in Manchuria; Kublai led an army against him, Nayan was smothered under felt carpets, and the uprisings of his supporters were ruthlessly repressed until 1289.

The revolt of Li Tan in 1262 left Kublai distrustful of ethnic Han. In 1279–1280 he decreed death for those who slaughtered animals according to Islamic or Jewish law. His monetary policy ended badly: the bills issued from 1273 to finance the Song war became, through lack of fiscal discipline and inflation, an economic disaster, and gold and silver were confiscated from citizens and foreign merchants in exchange for notes.

Against the advice of some Confucian-trained advisers he invaded Japan, Burma, Vietnam and Java. The fleets sent to Japan in 1274 and 1281 were destroyed, and the Java expedition of 1293 withdrew with the loss of more than 3,000 troops. In Tibet his grandson Buqa-Temür killed 10,000 Tibetans in crushing the Drikung Kagyu in 1291.
sections.last:
After the death of his wife Chabi in 1281 Kublai began to withdraw from direct contact with his advisers and issued instructions through another of his queens, Nambui. His chosen successor was his son Zhenjin, who headed the Zhongshu Sheng and administered the dynasty in Confucian fashion. In 1285 an official proposed that Kublai abdicate in Zhenjin's favour; the suggestion angered Kublai, who refused to see his son, and Zhenjin died soon afterwards, eight years before his father. Kublai regretted this and remained very close to Zhenjin's wife, Bairam, also known as Kokejin.

Kublai grew increasingly despondent after the deaths of his favourite wife and his heir, and the failure of the campaigns in Vietnam and Japan also haunted him. He turned to food and drink, became grossly overweight and suffered from gout and diabetes; his overindulgence in alcohol and the meat-rich Mongol diet may have contributed to the gout. He tried every treatment available, from Korean shamans to Vietnamese doctors, to no avail.

At the end of 1293 the emperor refused to take part in the traditional New Year's ceremony. Before his death he passed the seal of Crown Prince to Zhenjin's son Temür, who became the next Khagan and the second ruler of the Yuan dynasty. The only old companion the palace staff could find to comfort him in his final illness was Bayan, more than 30 years his junior. Kublai weakened steadily and died on 18 February 1294 at the age of 78. Two days later the funeral cortège took his body to the burial place of the Khans in Mongolia.
sections.legacy:
Kublai's seizure of power in 1260 pushed the Mongol Empire in a new direction. The controversy over his accession accelerated the disunity of the Mongols: his real power was limited to the Yuan Empire, though as Khagan he still influenced the Ilkhanate and, to a much lesser degree, the Golden Horde, and the Kublaids kept suzerainty over the Ilkhans until the end of their regime. His willingness to identify the Mongol-ruled realm as China brought the empire to international attention, and his conquests and those of his predecessors were largely responsible for re-creating a unified, militarily powerful China. Yuan rule of Tibet, Manchuria and Mongolia from a capital at modern Beijing set a precedent for the Qing dynasty's expansion into Inner Asia.

Under Kublai direct contact between East Asia and Europe was established, made possible by Mongol control of the Central Asian trade routes and by efficient postal services. His paper money was later imitated by Gaykhatu of the Ilkhanate, a complete failure.

The invasions of Vietnam are judged differently: several scholars treat them as a success because tributary relations were established, while Vietnamese historiography regards the war as a major victory over foreign invaders. Of the attempts on Japan, David Nicolle wrote that “the myth of Mongol invincibility had been shattered throughout eastern Asia”; the maritime archaeologist Kenzo Hayashida, who found the wreckage of the second fleet, concluded that Kublai had rushed its construction.

summary: Kublai Khan (1215–1294), grandson of Genghis Khan, was proclaimed Great Khan in 1260 and defeated his brother Ariq Böke in a civil war that began the division of the Mongol Empire. He founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and by 1279 ruled all of China. His invasions of Japan, Vietnam and Java failed.
references: Morris Rossabi, Khubilai Khan: His Life and Times (University of California Press, 1988)
John Man, Kublai Khan: The Mongol King Who Remade China (Bantam Press, 2007)
Jonathan Clements, A Brief History of Khubilai Khan (Running Press, 2010)
Christopher Pratt Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire (Facts On File, 2004)
notes: Proclamation as Great Khan: the article gives 15 April 1260 (Enthronement) and 'proclaimed Khagan at his residence in Shangdu on 5 May 1260' (Capital city); 15 April used in 'rise', the event gives only the year.

Zhenjin's death: the text says he 'died soon afterward in 1286, eight years before his father'; the family list gives 1240–1285 (and his birth as 1240, while the early-years section has Haiyun naming the son 'born in 1243'). No year stated in 'last'; birth year left out.
Song: the article says the imperial family surrendered in 1276 and the last loyalists were crushed 'three years later'; elsewhere 1279 at Yamen. Both used.

Second invasion of Japan: the article says the fleet sailed 'in November' but the Korean fleet reached Hakata Bay on 23 June 1281; months left out. Troop and ship figures (900 ships/40,000; 3,500 ships/100,000; about 3,500 Mongol dead) left out as the passage is confused.
Genghis Khan's death: the lede says Kublai was 'almost 12', the body '12' in 1227; left out. The 1224 hunt: 'nine years old' kept as the article has it (birth in 1215).
Goryeo: the article says Kublai 'enthroned Wonjong (r. 1260–1274) in 1259' and made Goryeo a tributary state in 1260; only the 1260 statement used.
Phagpa: the article says he was appointed Imperial Preceptor and, separately, 'promoted to imperial preceptor' in 1270 after creating the script; no year given in the text.

The trebuchet engineers: called 'two Iraqi siege engineers from the Ilkhanate' and named Ismail and Al al-Din in another section; the article says they 'invented' the Muslim trebuchet with Kublai, which is put here only as their trebuchets being used at Xiangyang.
Hayashida's wreck site is given as 'Takashima District, Shiga' in the article (doubtful); the place is left out.

The Legacy section of the article is three sentences; the legacy section here draws also on the lede and the reign sections. The article does not give his birthplace, the cause of death beyond the decline described, or the later history of the Yuan beyond its fall to the Ming in 1368.
Vietnam invasions listed with differing dates in the article (1258, 1285, 1287–1288; 'five incursions between 1257 and 1292'); kept general.
References: books about the person from the article's own bibliography sections (scripts/kinds/article-refs.js, or its Further reading list), chosen by the editor.
